title: China's churches
hookLine: registered and house churches, growing through persecution

lines: A CHURCH WITH ITS NAME ON THE GATE.
AN APARTMENT WITH THE CURTAINS DRAWN.
THE SAME GOSPEL IN BOTH ROOMS.
cards: Two Sunday mornings in the same Chinese city. In the first, a church with its name on the gate: doors open, choir robed, hymn numbers on a board at the front, registered with the state.
In the second, an apartment a few streets away. Curtains drawn. Folding chairs borrowed from neighbors who don't ask questions.
Someone keeps the singing soft. Both rooms are reading the same Gospel. Both are being watched, in different ways.

teach.b: Christians in China gather in roughly two ways. Registered churches belong to bodies the government recognizes, and meet openly under state rules about what can be taught and who can attend.
House churches meet outside that system, in homes, offices, rented rooms. The line between them isn't always neat, and Christians in China disagree about it honestly.
Some register so they can worship in the open and serve within the law. Others refuse, because they won't let the state decide what happens in worship.
Reports from China describe hard seasons for both: crosses taken down from church roofs, gatherings closed, pastors detained. And still the people keep meeting.
Nobody can count them exactly; a church in a living room keeps no public list. Jesus talked about growth you can't watch.

teach.h: A CORN OF WHEAT FALLS INTO THE GROUND.
teach.b: In John's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." A corn of wheat is just a grain.
It goes under before anything comes up.
And in Mark, a man scatters seed and goes to bed, and it grows while he sleeps and wakes: "the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how." The farmer isn't in charge of it.

An old saying, traced to an early Christian writer named Tertullian, says the blood of Christians is seed. Christians in China wouldn't all put it that way, and the old line is no reason to romanticize suffering.
Some readers hear the same picture in what Jesus said: under the ground is not the same as gone.

how: Some Christians elsewhere pray for the church in China in their own prayers and in services; in China, registered congregations meet in church buildings, while house churches gather in homes and other private spaces.

games.q: a man scatters seed on the ground, then goes to bed. in Jesus's parable in Mark, what happens next?
o: he stays up digging to check on it.
it springs and grows while he sleeps, he knows not how.
the birds eat all of it before morning.
games.why: the seed grows night and day, "he knoweth not how." the growing happens in the dark, without him in charge of it.

practice: Picture the two rooms from the start, and someone in each: an older woman with a worn Bible, a young man keeping one eye on the door. You don't know their names; hold them anyway.
If you pray, pray for Christians in China in both kinds of room, in whatever words you have; if not, simply wish them safety and courage.

wordCard.voice: China's churches. Registered churches meeting in the open, and house churches meeting outside registration: two ways of gathering, under pressure, around the same Gospel.
